passages.t: ‘Let everything that has breath praise the LORD’: the last word
passages.happening:
Psalm 150 is the last psalm in the book, and it is all praise. After the opening ‘Hallelujah’, every line until the last begins with ‘Praise’.

Where? “Hallelujah! Praise God in His sanctuary. Praise Him in His mighty heavens” (verse 1). On earth and in heaven.

Why? “Praise Him for His mighty acts; praise Him for His excellent greatness” (verse 2). For what he has done and for who he is.

How? With everything there is. “Praise Him with the sound of the horn; praise Him with the harp and lyre” (verse 3). “Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; praise Him with strings and flute” (verse 4). “Praise Him with clashing cymbals; praise Him with resounding cymbals” (verse 5).

Who? “Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Hallelujah!” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The instruments come from every part of Israel's life. The horn, the shofar, was a ram's horn blown for feasts, for gatherings and for the crowning of a king. Harp and lyre were played by the temple musicians. The tambourine and dancing belonged to ordinary people at celebrations. Cymbals rang out loud. The psalm puts the solemn and the joyful, the priest and the crowd, into one sound.

The book page notes that the Hebrew name of the book is Tehillim, ‘praises’, and that many readers take the five Hallelujah psalms as the close of the whole book. Psalm 150 is its last word, and that word is praise.

Notice who is invited at the end. Not only Israel, and not only people, but ‘everything that has breath’. God breathed the breath of life into the first man (Genesis 2:7). Every breath he gives can come back to him as praise.
passages.later:
The New Testament's only ‘Hallelujah’ comes in Revelation, where a great crowd in heaven shouts it four times: “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns” (Revelation 19:6).

The Psalms did not stop at Psalm 150. Jesus prayed them, to his last breath on the cross: “Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit” (Luke 23:46), from Psalm 31:5. And the first churches took them up as their own songs. Paul told them, “Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” (Ephesians 5:19).
passages.asks:
Do you have breath? Then Psalm 150 is speaking to you.

You do not need to feel like praising to begin. Many of the psalms before this one began in the dark. You may simply add your breath to the sound, today, and let the last word of the Psalms be yours as well: ‘Let everything that has breath praise the LORD.’

From here the Psalms go on in the prayers of Jesus and of his church, which still prays and sings them.
